text:
I stood there with my keys in my hand for a long time. Then I stepped carefully over the prints, went inside, and locked the door twice.

By seven I was standing on the sidewalk with a coffee I did not want, while across the street Hale watered his tomatoes the way he did every morning. He was eighty years old and thin as a rake, and he noticed everything that happened on our street.

"You look absolutely terrible," Hale said, and he lowered the hose until it dripped quietly on his shoes.

I described the camera and the recordings, but I left out the footprints, because saying them aloud made me feel ridiculous. He listened with his head tilted and asked me what time the notification came. I told him it was 3:12 every night.

He was silent for a moment. "My wife used to say that the dead keep appointments," he finally said, "and I never believed her. Buy a motion light, and buy a second camera, because if somebody is out there, you should see them from two directions."

It was sensible advice, so that afternoon I drove to the hardware store and bought both of them. I spent several hours on a ladder, fastening a bright motion light above the door. Then I mounted a second camera at the corner of the porch roof, aimed down the length of the boards.

By evening everything worked perfectly, so I changed into my uniform and drove to the hospital. At 3:12 I was alone at the nurses' station, recording a patient's blood pressure, when my phone chimed. I opened the application with a dry mouth.

There were two recordings this time. In the first, the figure stood motionless in its hood, and the new motion light never came on. In the second, the side angle showed the open doorway behind it, and beyond the doorway was my front hall.

The hall light was on. I never leave it on, not even once.
summary: She tells her elderly neighbor Hale, buys a motion light and a second camera, and the new recording shows the hall light inside her house switched on, which she never does.
